The Kalahari Desert. A large semi-arid sandy savanna covering roughly three hundred sixty thousand square miles across Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa. Unlike hot deserts, it receives enough seasonal rainfall to support scattered grassland, shrub, and hardy trees, and is home to diverse wildlife and the indigenous San people who have inhabited it for millennia.

Characterized by red sand dunes and sparse vegetation, the Kalahari is considerably less barren than the Sahara or Atacama. It features seasonal water sources and underground aquifers that sustain life in ways true deserts cannot. The Okavango Delta, the world's largest inland delta, borders it to the north, creating a seasonal flood-fed ecosystem that supports massive wildlife concentrations.

The Kalahari is home to lions, African wild dogs, meerkats, and other predators. Wildlife documentaries including Planet Earth and The Life of Mammals have featured its ecosystems. The San people, also called Bushmen, have lived as hunter-gatherers in the Kalahari for at least twenty thousand years. Their deep ecological knowledge of its plants and animals represents one of humanity's oldest continuous cultures.

Named from the Khoi word meaning the great thirst, the Kalahari reflects its low and erratic rainfall despite not being a true desert in technical terms. The Central Kalahari Game Reserve, established in nineteen sixty-one, is one of Africa's largest protected areas. Ground-nesting birds like the secretary bird and social weavers thrive in its open grassland habitat.

The San people's millennia of adaptation to the environment make them the indigenous custodians of this landscape. The Okavango Delta stands as a neighboring ecosystem of striking contrast to the drier Kalahari proper. Iconic refuges for predators and grazing herbivores, these spaces anchor the ecological heart of southern Africa's interior.
